# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# Apply practical column widths, filters, frozen headers, and
# clickable source URLs to one worksheet in the V8.1 Excel snapshot.
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
def format_excel_sheet(
    writer,
    sheet_name,
    dataframe,
    url_column="original_pdf_url"
):
    workbook = writer.book

    worksheet = writer.sheets[
        sheet_name
    ]

    # Freeze only the header row.
    worksheet.freeze_panes(
        1,
        0
    )

    worksheet.set_zoom(
        90
    )

    header_format = workbook.add_format({
        "bold": True,
        "text_wrap": True,
        "valign": "top",
        "border": 1,
    })

    url_format = workbook.add_format({
        "font_color": "blue",
        "underline": 1,
    })

    high_review_format = workbook.add_format({
        "bold": True,
    })

    for col_num, column_name in enumerate(
        dataframe.columns
    ):
        worksheet.write(
            0,
            col_num,
            column_name,
            header_format
        )

    worksheet.set_row(
        0,
        34
    )

    if len(
        dataframe.columns
    ):
        worksheet.autofilter(
            0,
            0,
            max(
                len(
                    dataframe
                ),
                1
            ),
            len(
                dataframe.columns
            )
            - 1
        )

    widths = {
        "filing_id": 13,
        "politician": 22,
        "member_status": 14,
        "state_district": 14,
        "source_pdf": 17,
        "source_year": 11,
        "transaction_number_in_filing": 17,
        "owner": 9,
        "asset": 34,
        "ticker": 11,
        "asset_type": 11,
        "transaction_type": 16,
        "transaction_date": 15,
        "notification_date": 16,
        "amount_min": 14,
        "amount_max": 14,
        "amount_exact": 14,
        "amount_category": 22,
        "amount_status": 19,
        "filing_status": 14,
        "subholding": 32,
        "location": 20,
        "description": 40,
        "comments": 55,
        "page": 9,
        "last_page": 10,
        "page_parse_method": 22,
        "page_recovery_used": 18,
        "filing_page_completeness_issue": 22,
        "suspected_missed_pages": 22,
        "page_continuation_used": 18,
        "duplicate_geometry_rows_merged": 20,
        "possible_adjacent_same_signature": 22,
        "row_shaded": 12,
        "geometry_quality_score": 17,
        "unicode_repair_applied": 18,
        "unicode_repair_count": 18,
        "needs_review": 13,
        "original_pdf_url": 42,
        "review_level": 12,
        "review_reason": 42,
        "owner_raw": 22,
        "asset_raw": 36,
        "asset_lookup_context": 38,
        "transaction_type_raw": 22,
        "transaction_date_raw": 22,
        "notification_date_raw": 22,
        "amount_raw": 22,
        "continuation_raw": 40,
        "detail_raw": 45,
        "pages_with_words": 16,
        "pages_with_geometry": 18,
        "table_pages": 12,
        "recovered_pages": 20,
        "suspected_missed_pages": 22,
        "geometry_error": 40,
    }

    for col_num, column_name in enumerate(
        dataframe.columns
    ):
        worksheet.set_column(
            col_num,
            col_num,
            widths.get(
                column_name,
                15
            )
        )

    # Make original PDF URL explicitly clickable.
    if (
        url_column
        in dataframe.columns
    ):
        url_col = dataframe.columns.get_loc(
            url_column
        )

        for row_num, value in enumerate(
            dataframe[
                url_column
            ].fillna(
                ""
            ).astype(
                str
            ),
            start=1
        ):
            if value.startswith(
                "http"
            ):
                worksheet.write_url(
                    row_num,
                    url_col,
                    value,
                    url_format,
                    string=value
                )

    # Emphasize high-review rows in the review_level column.
    if (
        "review_level"
        in dataframe.columns
        and len(
            dataframe
        )
    ):
        review_col = dataframe.columns.get_loc(
            "review_level"
        )

        worksheet.conditional_format(
            1,
            review_col,
            len(
                dataframe
            ),
            review_col,
            {
                "type": "text",
                "criteria": "containing",
                "value": "high",
                "format": high_review_format,
            }
        )


with pd.ExcelWriter(
    OUTPUT_XLSX,
    engine="xlsxwriter",
    engine_kwargs={
        "options": {
            "strings_to_urls": False
        }
    }
) as writer:
    transactions_v8.to_excel(
        writer,
        index=False,
        sheet_name="Transactions"
    )

    fallback_v8.to_excel(
        writer,
        index=False,
        sheet_name="Needs Fallback"

    format_excel_sheet(
        writer,
        "Transactions",
        transactions_v8
    )

    format_excel_sheet(
        writer,
        "Needs Fallback",
        fallback_v8
    )

    "Workbook refreshed:"
)

print(
    OUTPUT_XLSX
)

text: When real-world violence escalates or de-escalates in the Iran conflict, does Donald Trump’s rhetoric on Truth Social shift in predictable ways — toward more threatening or victorious language before/during high-fatality events, and toward more diplomatic or ceasefire-oriented language afterward?

title: Political Text Analysis
text:
Data
Two sources are aligned by date:

Trump’s Truth Social posts. The full public archive of his original posts (not reblogs) is pulled from a Hugging Face dataset, filtered to calendar-year 2026 and to posts mentioning Iran (401 posts YTD as of this snapshot).
UCDP conflict events. The Uppsala Conflict Data Program’s Georeferenced Event Dataset, filtered to events with US or joint US–Israel involvement related to the Iran conflict (through July 2026). UCDP is manually researcher-coded from primary reporting on organized violence, which makes it a more reliable “ground truth” for event timing and severity than automated event trackers like GDELT, though its inclusion rule (battle-related fatalities) means it can miss purely diplomatic or political moments that don’t involve violence.

For each UCDP event, a 1-day event window (day before / day of / day after, in Eastern time) is built around it, and any Iran-related Trump posts falling in that window are attached. This produces 393 unique event-dates with matched posts, spanning 543 underlying UCDP event records.
Each event-date is also assigned a significance level (Standard, Notable, High, Major, or Context) from same-day UCDP record count, best fatality estimate, and civilian death count — e.g., 2026-02-28 and 2026-04-06 are both coded “Major” based on same-day death tolls in the dozens to low hundreds.

title: Political Text Analysis
text:
Approach

Collect Trump’s Truth Social posts (Hugging Face archive) and UCDP’s Iran-conflict event records (filtered Excel export), both refreshed periodically as new data becomes available.
Window the two datasets together: for every UCDP event, pull Iran-related posts from the day before, day of, and day after.
Score rhetoric with zero-shot classification. A Hugging Face multi-label zero-shot classifier scores each post’s content_text — and only the text, never the UCDP metadata — against four labels: Threat, Victory, Diplomacy, and Ceasefire/Ending, each a continuous 0–1 probability.
Aggregate event-balanced means. Because posting volume varies a lot day to day, scores are first averaged within each event, then averaged across events — so a single high-volume posting day doesn’t dominate the pattern.
Visualize the result as a connected, per-event timeline: each UCDP event sits at a central node sized/colored by significance, with the day-before/day-of/day-after posts and their four rhetorical scores branching around it.

title: Political Text Analysis
text:
Limitations

Small sample. 103 posts were actually scored (many event-windows have no matching Trump post at all), and results should be read as a descriptive pattern within one leader’s rhetoric during one specific conflict, not a generalizable claim.
Zero-shot labels are heuristic. The classifier was never fine-tuned on this domain; label probabilities reflect a general-purpose model’s association between text and label names, not a validated measure of intent or sentiment.
UCDP’s fatality-based inclusion criterion means the event set may under-represent diplomatically significant moments (sanctions, negotiation breakdowns) that didn’t involve violence — so “no nearby UCDP event” doesn’t mean “nothing happened.”
Correlational, not causal. Matching rhetoric to nearby events shows co-occurrence, not that either caused the other — Trump may be reacting to the same news coverage the event is drawn from, rather than reacting to the event’s severity per se.
Both the Truth Social archive and the UCDP extract are periodic snapshots (current through mid-2026), not a live feed; this page will be refreshed as new data comes in this semester.

title: Stage 1 of 4 — Download Official House PTR PDFs From the House XML Filing Index
text:
4. Download the PTRs
For each year, this cell:

Downloads the House financial-disclosure XML index.
Looks through every filing.
Keeps only filings where FilingType is P (only want PTRs).
Gets the DocID.
Builds the PTR PDF URL.
Checks whether that PDF already exists in Google Drive.
Downloads it only if it is missing.


Code walkthrough — discover PTRs and download PDFs
This is the main Stage 1 loop.
For each year it:

Downloads <YEAR>FD.xml from the House Clerk.
Parses every <Member> filing record.
Keeps only FilingType == "P".
Reads the filing DocID.
Builds the official PTR PDF URL.
Skips the file if it is already in Drive.
Downloads missing PDFs.
Prints counts for listed, downloaded, and already-present files.

The existing code already contains line-by-line comments; those comments are retained.

# ============================================================================
# STAGE 1 — MAIN DOWNLOADER
# ============================================================================
# Discover official PTR DocIDs from the annual House XML index and download missing source PDFs. Existing PDFs are deliberately left untouched.

# BASE_FOLDER is the main folder where all downloaded PTR PDFs will be saved.
# Path() makes it easier to work with folders and filenames in Python.
PROJECT_ROOT = Path("/content/drive/MyDrive/Congressional Trading Data/House_PTRs")
BASE_FOLDER = PROJECT_ROOT / "01 Official House PTR PDFs"

# Create the descriptive source-PDF archive folder if it does not already exist.
# parents=True means Python can also create any missing parent folders.
# exist_ok=True means don't throw an error if the folder already exists.
BASE_FOLDER.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)


# Some websites behave differently depending on what kind of browser/program
# is making the request.
#
# This tells the House website that our request looks like it came from
# a normal web browser instead of an unidentified Python script.
headers = {
    "User-Agent": "Mozilla/5.0"
}


# Loop through every year in our YEARS list.
#
# Example:
# YEARS = [2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026]
#
# First year = 2021
# then 2022
# then 2023
# etc.
for year in YEARS:

    # Print a visual divider so we can easily see which year is being processed.
    #
    # The f before the string lets us insert the value of year using {year}.
    # \n means start with a new line.
    print(f"\n===== {year} =====")


    # Build the URL for that year's House financial disclosure XML file.
    #
    # If year = 2026, this becomes:
    #
    # https://disclosures-clerk.house.gov/
    # public_disc/financial-pdfs/2026FD.xml
    xml_url = (
        f"https://disclosures-clerk.house.gov/"
        f"public_disc/financial-pdfs/{year}FD.xml"
    )


    # Just tell us what the program is doing.
    print("Downloading filing index...")


    # requests.get() downloads information from a URL.
    #
    # xml_url = the address we want
    # headers=headers = send the browser-style User-Agent above
    #
    # The result gets stored in the variable response.
    response = requests.get(xml_url, headers=headers)


    # Check whether the download succeeded.
    #
    # If the website returns something like:
    # 404 = file not found
    # 500 = server error
    #
    # this line stops the program and shows the error.
    response.raise_for_status()


    # response.content contains the actual XML file we just downloaded.
    #
    # ET = xml.etree.ElementTree
    #
    # ET.fromstring() reads the XML and turns it into a structure
    # Python can search through.
    root = ET.fromstring(response.content)


    # Create a folder specifically for this year.
    #
    # If:
    # BASE_FOLDER = Congressional Trading Data/House_PTRs/01 Official House PTR PDFs
    # year = 2026
    #
    # then year_folder becomes:
    #
    # Congressional Trading Data/House_PTRs/01 Official House PTR PDFs/2026
    year_folder = BASE_FOLDER / str(year)


    # Create the year's folder if it does not already exist.
    year_folder.mkdir(exist_ok=True)


    # These are counters so we can see what happened when the program finishes.
    #
    # Start all three at zero.
    total_ptrs = 0
    downloaded = 0
    skipped = 0


    # Look through every XML element named "Member".
    #
    # Each Member entry represents one financial disclosure filing.
    for member in root.iter("Member"):


        # Find the FilingType field inside this Member entry.
        #
        # Example:
        # <FilingType>P</FilingType>
        #
        # filing_type would then equal:
        # "P"
        filing_type = member.findtext("FilingType")


        # Find the DocID field.
        #
        # Example:
        # <DocID>20034567</DocID>
        #
        # doc_id would then equal:
        # "20034567"
        doc_id = member.findtext("DocID")


        # We only care about PTRs.
        #
        # P = Periodic Transaction Report
        #
        # != means "does not equal"
        #
        # So:
        # if filing_type is NOT "P"
        # skip the rest of this loop and move to the next filing.
        if filing_type != "P":
            continue


        # Make sure the filing actually has a DocID.
        #
        # "if not doc_id" means:
        # if doc_id is missing or empty.
        #
        # Without a DocID we cannot build the PDF URL.
        if not doc_id:
            continue


        # If we got this far, we know this filing is a PTR with a DocID.
        #
        # Add 1 to our total PTR count.
        total_ptrs += 1


        # Decide where this PDF should be saved.
        #
        # Example:
        #
        # year_folder = Congressional Trading Data/House_PTRs/01 Official House PTR PDFs/2026
        # doc_id = 20034567
        #
        # pdf_path becomes:
        #
        # Congressional Trading Data/House_PTRs/01 Official House PTR PDFs/2026/20034567.pdf
        pdf_path = year_folder / f"{doc_id}.pdf"


        # Check whether we already have this PDF.
        #
        # .exists() returns:
        # True  = file exists
        # False = file does not exist
        if pdf_path.exists():

            # Count it as a skipped file.
            skipped += 1

            # Move immediately to the next filing.
            #
            # This is what prevents us from downloading duplicates.
            continue


        # Build the URL for the actual PTR PDF.
        #
        # Example:
        #
        # year = 2026
        # doc_id = 20034567
        #
        # becomes:
        #
        # https://disclosures-clerk.house.gov/
        # public_disc/ptr-pdfs/2026/20034567.pdf
        pdf_url = (
            f"https://disclosures-clerk.house.gov/"
            f"public_disc/ptr-pdfs/{year}/{doc_id}.pdf"
        )


        # try means:
        #
        # "Attempt this code, but if something goes wrong,
        # don't crash the whole program."
        try:


            # Download the actual PDF.
            #
            # timeout=30 means:
            # if the website does not respond within 30 seconds,
            # give up on this particular request.
            pdf_response = requests.get(
                pdf_url,
                headers=headers,
                timeout=30
            )


            # Make sure the PDF download succeeded.
            #
            # If we get a 404, 500, etc., this creates an error
            # that gets handled by the except section below.
            pdf_response.raise_for_status()


            # pdf_response.content contains the actual bytes of the PDF.
            #
            # write_bytes() saves those bytes as a file in Google Drive.
            pdf_path.write_bytes(pdf_response.content)


            # We successfully downloaded one PDF,
            # so increase the downloaded counter by 1.
            downloaded += 1


            # Show us which DocID was downloaded.
            print("Downloaded:", doc_id)


            # Pause for half a second before requesting another PDF.
            #
            # This avoids hammering the House website with requests
            # as fast as Python possibly can.
            time.sleep(0.5)


        # If anything inside the try block fails,
        # Python jumps down here instead of killing the whole program.
        except Exception as error:


            # Print which DocID failed and the error message.
            #
            # Then the loop continues on to the next filing.
            print("ERROR:", doc_id, error)


    # Print a blank line after finishing the year.
    print()


    # Show how many PTR records existed in the XML.
    print("PTRs listed:", total_ptrs)


    # Show how many new PDFs we actually downloaded.
    print("Downloaded:", downloaded)


    # Show how many PDFs were already in Drive and therefore skipped.
    print("Already had:", skipped)


    # Show the folder where this year's PDFs were saved.
    print("Saved in:", year_folder)

section: Why this is separate from the PDF parser
text:
Why this is separate from the PDF parser
These are two different questions:

Extraction: what text did the House PDF publish?
Resolution: which parenthetical text is actually the security ticker?

Keeping them separate makes ticker decisions reversible and prevents a small ticker-rule change from forcing another multi-hour pass over thousands of PDFs.

title: Stage 4 of 4 — Clean and Resolve Ticker Edge Cases From the V8.1 Transaction CSV (V8.2)
text:
Conservative V8.2 rule
For stock ([ST]) rows:
preserved asset evidence
        ↓
use only text BEFORE the first [ST]
        ↓
take the last compact parenthetical
        ↓
preserve it as ticker_candidate_raw
        ↓
accept strong structural candidate
or mark uncertain candidate for review
This specifically prevents later detail text such as a subholding (BM) from overwriting an actual asset ticker such as (META).
V8.2 also avoids semantic blacklists that previously caused legitimate symbols such as ETN, ADS, FUND, and CORP to disappear.

    out_df.columns.get_loc("asset") + 1,

    out_df["asset"]
)

    axis=1,

out_df["ticker"] = out_df[
    "ticker_resolved"

out_df.drop(

)

out_df["asset"] = out_df.apply(
    lambda row: remove_resolved_ticker_from_asset(
        row["asset_v8_1"],
        row["ticker"]
    ),
    axis=1
)

out_df["ticker_changed"] = (
    out_df["ticker"]
        .fillna("")
        .astype(str)
        .str.upper()
    !=
    out_df["ticker_v8_1"]
        .fillna("")
        .astype(str)
        .str.upper()
)

out_df["asset_changed_by_ticker_resolver"] = (
    out_df["asset"]
        .fillna("")
        .astype(str)
    !=
    out_df["asset_v8_1"]

        .astype(str)
)

review_updates = out_df.apply(

)

for column in [

]:

    out_df["review_reason_v8_1"]

    old_missing_ticker
    & out_df["ticker"]
        .fillna("")
        .astype(str)
        .str.strip()
        .ne("")

    pd.to_numeric(

            fixed_missing_ticker,
            "geometry_quality_score"
        ],
        errors="coerce"
    )
    .fillna(100)
    .add(5)
    .clip(upper=100)
)

section: How the master executes a child notebook
text:
How the master executes a child notebook
The function below intentionally executes code cells only.
Markdown cells are documentation and therefore do not need to run.
Each child code cell runs through get_ipython().run_cell(...), which is important because Stage 3 contains a %pip magic command that ordinary Python exec() would not understand.
The function checks IPython’s execution result after every cell. If a cell fails, the master raises an error with the stage/cell number instead of continuing with incomplete data.

# =============================================================================
# MASTER EXECUTOR — RUN ONE .IPYNB INSIDE THE CURRENT COLAB RUNTIME
# =============================================================================

def run_notebook_in_current_runtime(notebook_path, stage_number, stage_title):
    """
    Execute the code cells from one notebook in this current Colab runtime.

    Why current-runtime execution is useful here:
    - the Drive mount is shared
    - variables/packages installed by earlier cells are immediately available
    - Stage 3's resumable checkpoint logic behaves exactly as when the notebook
      is run directly
    - IPython/Colab magics such as %pip still work
    """

    notebook_path = Path(notebook_path)

    print()
    print("=" * 90)
    print(f"STARTING STAGE {stage_number}: {stage_title}")
    print(notebook_path)
    print("=" * 90)

    # Read the .ipynb file. A notebook is JSON containing ordered cell objects.
    with notebook_path.open(
        "r",
        encoding="utf-8"
    ) as handle:
        notebook = json.load(handle)

    # Keep only executable code cells. Markdown is explanatory documentation.
    code_cells = [
        cell
        for cell in notebook.get("cells", [])
        if cell.get("cell_type") == "code"
    ]

    print(
        f"Executable code cells in Stage {stage_number}:",
        len(code_cells)
    )

    stage_started = time.time()

    for code_index, cell in enumerate(
        code_cells,
        start=1
    ):
        source = "".join(
            cell.get("source", [])
        )

        # Empty code cells do not need to be sent to IPython.
        if not source.strip():
            continue

        print()
        print(
            f"[Stage {stage_number}] "
            f"Running code cell {code_index}/{len(code_cells)}"
        )

        # run_cell() understands ordinary Python plus Colab/IPython magics.
        result = get_ipython().run_cell(
            source,
            store_history=False
        )

        # IPython normally captures exceptions in the ExecutionResult rather
        # than automatically raising them back to this outer loop.
        error = (
            getattr(result, "error_before_exec", None)
            or getattr(result, "error_in_exec", None)
        )

        if error is not None:
            raise RuntimeError(
                f"Stage {stage_number} failed in child code cell "
                f"{code_index}: {error}"
            ) from error

    elapsed_minutes = (
        time.time() - stage_started
    ) / 60.0

    print()
    print("=" * 90)
    print(
        f"FINISHED STAGE {stage_number}: {stage_title}"
    )
    print(
        f"Elapsed: {elapsed_minutes:.1f} minutes"
    )
    print("=" * 90)

This repo and the sibling senate-ptr-scraper repo are wired up to scrape Senate PTR data and rebuild/deploy this site automatically. A few steps can only be done by you in the GitHub UI (not something an assistant can do via local tools) — do these once to turn the automation on.
